title: The Triangle fire (1911)
hookLine: a fire in a garment factory takes young immigrant workers' lives, and labor laws follow

cards: Late on a Saturday afternoon, near quitting time, on the top floors of a building in Manhattan. Rows of sewing machines.
Young women bent over shirtwaists, the blouses of the day, with scraps of cotton piled under the tables. Someone shouts that there's a fire. The scraps catch like paper.
Workers run for the stairs, the elevator, the doors. And one of the doors won't open. It's locked.
Today's word is the name of that factory, and of that afternoon: the Triangle fire.

teach.b: The Triangle Waist Company made shirtwaists, and the people who sewed them were immigrants, among them young Jewish and Italian women from the streets of yesterday.

Doors were kept locked, it was said, to stop workers from slipping out or taking things. When the fire came, a locked door, a collapsing fire escape and ladders that couldn't reach high enough left workers trapped.
Some died inside. Some jumped. Crowds in the street watched it happen.
This lesson stays there only as long as it takes to honor them.
Then the city mourned. Mourners marched in the rain behind the coffins of the unclaimed dead.

A young labor organizer, Rose Schneiderman, stood up at a public meeting and told the city it had failed these workers, and that working people would have to save themselves. And something did change.
New York set up an investigation that went factory to factory, and new laws followed: fire exits and drills, sprinklers, and limits on hours.
The Torah has a line that sits right under this story: "Neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." Not just: don't harm. Don't stand by when someone else is in danger.
The same chapter says a worker's wages must not sit with you overnight.
Remembering the workers means asking who is behind the locked door today.
And this whole week has been about newcomers: a language carried from Spain, refugees at New Amsterdam, a letter, a great wave, a poet, a neighborhood, and today, a fire that rewrote the rules.

how: Each year in New York the Triangle fire is remembered at the site, where the workers' names are read aloud, and Jewish labor groups and synagogues have joined in marking the day.

practice: Bring to mind the workers of that afternoon, young women and men who came for a better life, and hold them in silence for a few breaths; if you pray, remember them in prayer.
Then think of one worker in your own world today whose safety or pay is easy to overlook.

wordCard.voice: Triangle fire. The garment factory fire behind a locked door that took young immigrant workers' lives and led to new laws for safer work. Today's word.
